claim: Primary sensory cortices can respond to stimuli of different sensory modalities.
source: A growing body of literature has demonstrated that primary sensory cortices are not exclusively unimodal, but can respond to stimuli of different sensory modalities.
evidence: Supported by citations to existing literature demonstrating cross-modal responses in primary sensory cortices.

claim: In untrained rats, the majority of GC neurons were modulated by a single modality.
source: We found that, in untrained rats, the majority of GC neurons were modulated by a single modality.
evidence: Based on experimental recordings and analysis of single unit responses in untrained rats.

claim: Upon learning, both prevalence of cross-modal responsive neurons and their breadth of tuning increased.
source: Upon learning, both prevalence of cross-modal responsive neurons and their breadth of tuning increased, leading to a greater overlap of representations.
evidence: Based on comparison of neural responses between untrained and trained rats.

claim: Learning changes the overlap of cross-modal representations in gustatory cortex.
source: Altogether, our results show that the gustatory cortex represents cross-modal stimuli according to their sensory identity, and that learning changes the overlap of cross-modal representations.
evidence: Based on experimental data comparing untrained and trained animals.

claim: Neurons in the visual cortex respond to acoustic stimuli.
source: Neurons in the visual cortex respond to acoustic stimuli (Iurilli et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: Activity in the auditory cortex is shaped by visual stimulation.
source: activity in the auditory cortex is also shaped by visual (Calvert et al., 1997; Brosch et al., 2005) and somatosensory stimulation (Zhou and Fuster, 2000; Schroeder et al., 2001; Fu et al., 2003; Brosch et al., 2005; Lakatos et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Activity in the auditory cortex is shaped by somatosensory stimulation.
source: activity in the auditory cortex is also shaped by visual (Calvert et al., 1997; Brosch et al., 2005) and somatosensory stimulation (Zhou and Fuster, 2000; Schroeder et al., 2001; Fu et al., 2003; Brosch et al., 2005; Lakatos et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Cross-modal responses have been observed in the olfactory cortex.
source: Similar results have been observed in the olfactory (Wesson and Wilson, 2010; Maier et al., 2012, 2015), gustatory (De Araujo and Rolls, 2004; Samuelsen et al., 2012; Gardner and Fontanini, 2014) and somatosensory cortices (Zhou and Fuster, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: Cross-modal responses have been observed in the gustatory cortex.
source: Similar results have been observed in the olfactory (Wesson and Wilson, 2010; Maier et al., 2012, 2015), gustatory (De Araujo and Rolls, 2004; Samuelsen et al., 2012; Gardner and Fontanini, 2014) and somatosensory cortices (Zhou and Fuster, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: Cross-modal responses have been observed in the somatosensory cortex.
source: Similar results have been observed in the olfactory (Wesson and Wilson, 2010; Maier et al., 2012, 2015), gustatory (De Araujo and Rolls, 2004; Samuelsen et al., 2012; Gardner and Fontanini, 2014) and somatosensory cortices (Zhou and Fuster, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: 33.3% of recorded GC neurons in untrained rats responded to at least one non-gustatory stimulus.
source: 33.3% [45/135] of recorded neurons responded to at least one non-gustatory stimulus
evidence: Based on experimental recordings and change point analysis in untrained rats, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 16.2% of GC neurons in untrained rats responded to odor.
evidence: Based on experimental recordings in untrained rats, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 15.5% of GC neurons in untrained rats responded to air puff.
evidence: Based on experimental recordings in untrained rats, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 4.4% of GC neurons in untrained rats responded to tone.
evidence: Based on experimental recordings in untrained rats, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 3.7% of GC neurons in untrained rats responded to light.
evidence: Based on experimental recordings in untrained rats, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Orofacial movements evoked by non-taste stimuli were significantly smaller compared to those evoked by tastants in untrained rats.
source: Orofacial movements evoked by non-taste stimuli were hardly detectable and significantly smaller compared to the ones evoked by tastants, indicating that they were not driving the changes in neuronal activity we observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Wilcoxon sign rank test: p<0.05).
evidence: Based on analysis of orofacial movements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C with statistical testing.

claim: Among non-gustatory stimuli, odors and somatosensory stimuli were most effective in modulating GC neurons in untrained rats.
source: Among the non-gustatory stimuli, odors and somatosensory stimuli appeared to be the most effective in modulating GC neurons.
evidence: Based on comparison of prevalence of responses to different cross-modal stimuli.

claim: The proportion of neurons responding to odorant and air puff were similar in untrained rats.
source: Specifically, while the proportion of neurons responding to odorant and air puff were similar (Figure 1A; Marascuillo's test, p>0.05)
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of response proportions shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The proportion of neurons responding to odorant and air puff were significantly higher compared to neurons responding to sound and light in untrained rats.
source: both were significantly higher compared to the proportion of neurons responding to sound and light (Figure 1A; Marascuillo's test, p>0.05)
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of response proportions shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 70.1% of taste selective neurons in untrained rats responded exclusively to gustatory stimuli.
source: Within the group of taste selective neurons (87/135), the majority responded exclusively to gustatory stimuli (Figure 1B, D–E; 70.1%, [61/87])
evidence: Based on analysis of taste selective neurons shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 25.3% of taste selective neurons in untrained rats were also activated by one cross-modal stimulus.
source: with only a few also activated by one (Figure 1B, F–G; 25.3%, [22/87])
evidence: Based on analysis of taste selective neurons shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 4.6% of taste selective neurons in untrained rats were also activated by two cross-modal stimuli.
source: or two (Figure 1B; 4.6%, [4/87]) cross modal stimuli
evidence: Based on analysis of taste selective neurons shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 84.4% of cross-modal responsive neurons in untrained rats were activated exclusively by one non-taste stimulus.
source: The majority of cross-modal neurons were activated exclusively by one of the non-taste stimuli (either air puff, odor, tone or light stimuli; Figure 1G; 84.4%, [38/45])
evidence: Based on analysis of cross-modal responsive neurons shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 11.1% of cross-modal responsive neurons in untrained rats responded to two cross-modal stimuli.
source: only a few neurons responded to two (11.1%, [5/45])
evidence: Based on analysis of cross-modal responsive neurons.

claim: 4.4% of cross-modal responsive neurons in untrained rats responded to three cross-modal stimuli.
source: or three (4.4%, [2/45]) cross-modal stimuli
evidence: Based on analysis of cross-modal responsive neurons.

claim: After 14 days of training, rats learned to associate each anticipatory cue with the delivery of sucrose.
source: Analysis of orofacial movements revealed that after 14 days of training rats learned to associate each anticipatory cue with the delivery of sucrose (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on analysis of conditioned orofacial movements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Conditioned orofacial movements were significantly stronger on the last day of training compared to the first day for somatosensory cues.
source: The conditioned orofacial movements were significantly stronger on the last day of training compared to the first day (Figure 2A; somatosensory: two-way ANOVA [factors: days and temporal epochs], F(1,2) = 43.8, p<0.01
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of orofacial movements across training days shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Conditioned orofacial movements were significantly stronger on the last day of training compared to the first day for odor cues.
source: odor: two-way ANOVA, F(1,2) = 45.3, p<0.01
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of orofacial movements across training days.

claim: Conditioned orofacial movements were significantly stronger on the last day of training compared to the first day for tone cues.
source: tone: two-way ANOVA, F(1,2) = 47.7, p<0.01
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of orofacial movements across training days.

claim: Conditioned orofacial movements were significantly stronger on the last day of training compared to the first day for light cues.
source: light: two-way ANOVA, F(1,2) = 76.6, p<0.01
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of orofacial movements across training days.

claim: Odor and somatosensory cues evoked mouth movements significantly larger than baseline on the third day of training.
source: Indeed, odor and somatosensory cues evoked mouth movements significantly larger than baseline (defined as orofacial movements on the first day of conditioning) on the third day of training (Figure 2B; p<0.05 with Tukey's correction).
evidence: Based on analysis of mouth movements across training days shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Visual and auditory cues required seven days of conditioning to display significant changes in orofacial movements.
source: In contrast, visual and auditory cues required seven days of conditioning to display significant changes in orofacial movements (Figure 2B; p<0.05 with Tukey's correction).
evidence: Based on analysis of mouth movements across training days shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The magnitude of mouth movements evoked by each anticipatory cue was not significantly different on the last day of conditioning.
source: Regardless of the difference in learning rate, the magnitude of the mouth movements evoked by each anticipatory cue was not significantly different on the last day of conditioning (one-way ANOVA [factor: cross-modal cues], F(3) = 2.24, p=0.12).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of mouth movements on the final day of training.

claim: Odors and somatosensory stimuli have higher associability to sucrose compared to visual and auditory cues.
source: Odors and somatosensory stimuli have a higher associability to sucrose compared to visual and auditory cues.
evidence: Based on differences in learning rates observed in behavioral data.

claim: Cue-taste association correlated with a significantly higher prevalence of neurons that responded to odor cues compared to untrained rats.
source: Indeed, cue-taste association correlated with a significantly higher prevalence of neurons that responded to cues of different sensory modalities compared to the group of untrained rats (Figure 4A; test for equality of proportion for all comparison; odor: 16.2% [22/135] untrained vs. 33.0% [39/118] trained, χ2(1) = 9.65, p<0.01
evidence: Based on comparison of neural responses between untrained and trained rats shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cue-taste association correlated with a significantly higher prevalence of neurons that responded to air puff cues compared to untrained rats.
evidence: Based on comparison of neural responses between untrained and trained rats.

claim: Cue-taste association correlated with a significantly higher prevalence of neurons that responded to tone cues compared to untrained rats.
evidence: Based on comparison of neural responses between untrained and trained rats.

claim: Cue-taste association correlated with a significantly higher prevalence of neurons that responded to light cues compared to untrained rats.
evidence: Based on comparison of neural responses between untrained and trained rats.

claim: Learning did not change the prevalence of taste selective neurons.
source: The increase was specific for responses to cross-modal stimuli, as learning did not change the prevalence of taste selective neurons (64.4% [87/135] for untrained vs. 57.6% [68/118] for trained, test for equality of proportion, χ2(1) = 1.23, p=0.26).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of taste selective neurons between untrained and trained rats.

claim: In trained rats, significantly more neurons responded to air puff and odor compared to light and sound.
source: Similarly conserved in trained rats was the bias for olfactory and somatosensory stimuli; indeed, significantly more neurons responded to air puff and odor compared to light and sound (Figure 3A, Marascuillo's test, p>0.05).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of response proportions in trained rats shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 50.7% of cue responsive neurons in trained rats were activated only by one out of four anticipatory cues.
source: Out of 69 neurons, which responded at least to one cross-modal stimulus, half of them (50.7%, [35/69]) were activated only by one out of four anticipatory cues (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on analysis of cue responsive neurons in trained rats shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 36.2% of cue responsive neurons in trained rats were responsive to two cues.
source: However, a substantial amount of cue responsive neurons were also responsive to two (36.2%, [25/69])
evidence: Based on analysis of cue responsive neurons in trained rats.

claim: 11.5% of cue responsive neurons in trained rats were responsive to three cues.
evidence: Based on analysis of cue responsive neurons in trained rats.

claim: 1.4% of cue responsive neurons in trained rats were responsive to four cues.
source: and four (1.4%, [1/69]) cues
evidence: Based on analysis of cue responsive neurons in trained rats.

claim: Trained rats showed a significant reduction in the number of single units responsive exclusively to taste compared to untrained rats.
source: When compared with untrained rats, trained rats showed a significant reduction in the number of single units responsive exclusively to taste (Figure 4B; 70.1% [61/87] for untrained and 39.7% [27/68] for trained rats: test for equality of proportion;χ2(1) = 14.38, p<0.001)
evidence: Based on statistical comparison between untrained and trained rats shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Trained rats showed a significant increase in the number of neurons responding to both taste and cues compared to untrained rats.
source: and a significant increase in the number of neurons responding to both taste and cues (Figure 4B; 33.3% [29/87] for untrained and 60.2% [41/68] for trained rats: test for equality of proportion;χ2(1) = 11.20, p<0.001)
evidence: Based on statistical comparison between untrained and trained rats shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In trained rats, fewer neurons were responsive only to one cue compared to untrained rats.
source: Specifically, in the trained groups of rats, we observed fewer neurons that were responsive only to one cue (Figure 4C; untrained: 84.4% [38/45]; trained: 50.7% [35/69]; test for equality of proportion;χ2(1) = 9.16, p<0.01)
evidence: Based on statistical comparison between untrained and trained rats shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In trained rats, more neurons were activated by two cues compared to untrained rats.
source: and more neurons that were activated by two cues (Figure 4C; untrained: 11.1% [5/45]; trained: 36.2% [25/69]; test for equality of proportion; χ2(1) = 5.60, p<0.05)
evidence: Based on statistical comparison between untrained and trained rats shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cue responsive neurons in trained rats did not display a preference for any specific tastant.
source: No bias toward any specific tastant was observed (cues/unexpected-sucrose 40.5% [28/69], cues/NaCl 37.6% [26/69], cues/citric acid 43.4% [30/69], cues/quinine 44.9% [31/69]; Pearson's χ2 test; χ2(3) = 0.36, p=0.94).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of tastant preferences in cue responsive neurons.

claim: Associative learning broadened the response tuning for taste selective neurons.
source: The results confirm that associative learning broadened the response tuning for both taste selective and cross-modal responsive neurons (taste selective neuron: 0.58 ± 0.02 and 0.48 ± 0.02 untrained and trained respectively, t-test: t(152) = −3.31; p<0.01
evidence: Based on comparison of sharpness indices between untrained and trained rats.

claim: Associative learning broadened the response tuning for cross-modal responsive neurons.
source: cross-modal responsive neurons: 0.60 ± 0.02 and 0.46 ± 0.01 untrained and trained respectively, t-test: t(107) = −4.77; p<0.01
evidence: Based on comparison of sharpness indices between untrained and trained rats.

claim: In trained rats, there was a reduction in the proportion of neurons that were excited by the cue compared to untrained rats.
source: In the group of trained animals we observed a reduction in the proportion of neurons that were excited by the cue (Figure 5A–B; 70.3% [38/54] for untrained vs. 52.2% [59/113] for trained, test for equality of proportion;χ2(1) = 4.30, p<0.05)
evidence: Based on analysis of excitatory and inhibitory responses shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: In trained rats, there was an increase in the proportion of neurons that were inhibited by the cue compared to untrained rats.
source: and an increase in the proportion of neurons that were inhibited by the cue (Figure 5A–B; rightmost panel; 29.6% [16/54] for untrained vs. 47.7% [54/113] for trained, test for equality of proportion;χ2(1) = 4.94, p<0.05)
evidence: Based on analysis of excitatory and inhibitory responses shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: In trained rats, cues evoked a significantly higher number of firing rate modulations per response compared to untrained animals.
source: In the group of trained rats, cues evoked a significantly higher number of firing rate modulation per response compared to what observed in untrained animals (1.22 ± 0.06 and 1.44 ± 0.07 for untrained and trained respectively; t-test: t(155) = −2.02; p<0.05) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on analysis of firing rate modulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: GC neurons in untrained rats can decode different stimulus modalities.
source: GC neurons were able to decode the different stimulus modalities both in untrained and trained rats (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: Based on decoding analysis shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: The peak classification performance for cross-modal stimuli was observed 100 ms after stimulus onset in untrained rats.
source: The peak classification performance was observed 100 ms after stimulus onset and was 0.67 for neurons in untrained rats
evidence: Based on decoding analysis of neural responses.

claim: The peak classification performance for cross-modal stimuli was 0.70 for neurons recorded in trained animals.
source: and 0.70 for neurons recorded in trained animals
evidence: Based on decoding analysis of neural responses.

claim: For untrained animals, the average of correct hits significantly outnumbered the average of false hits after stimulus onset.
source: After onset and after offset of cross-modal stimuli, the average of correct hits significantly outnumbered the average of false hits (Figure 6C; stimulus onset: 0.67 ± 0.16 and 0.26 ± 0.16 correct and false hits respectively; t-test: t(6) = 3.54; p<0.05
evidence: Based on decoding analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: For untrained animals, the average of correct hits significantly outnumbered the average of false hits after stimulus offset.
source: Figure 6D; stimulus offset: 0.48 ± 0.03 and 0.25 ± 0.04 correct and false hits respectively; t-test: t(6) = 5.31; p<0.05
evidence: Based on decoding analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: For trained animals, after cue onset, correct hits dramatically outnumbered false hits.
source: After cue onset, activity allowed for optimal coding of stimulus identity, with correct hits dramatically outnumbering false hits (Figure 6E; 0.70 ± 0.17 and 0.18 ± 0.02 correct and false hits respectively; t-test: t(6) = 5.89; p<0.05).
evidence: Based on decoding analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: For trained animals, after cue offset, neural activity led to an equally large number of correct and false hits.
source: After the offset of the cue, i.e., in the delay interval (500 ms) preceding sucrose delivery, neural activity lead to an equally large number of correct and false hits (Figure 6F; 0.45 ± 0.09 and 0.38 ± 0.04 correct and false hits respectively; t-test: t(6) = 1.11; p=0.30).
evidence: Based on decoding analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In trained animals, the decoder was more likely to confound stimuli that shared similar associability during the delay period.
source: It is important to notice that cross-modal stimuli were not randomly misclassified. Indeed the decoder was more likely to confound stimuli that shared similar associability. During the delay period, olfactory and somatosensory cues (the strongly associable cues, as determined by the faster learning rate in the behavioral experiment) could be easily confused with each other; similarly, visual and auditory cues (the two stimuli with weaker associability) could be misclassified.
evidence: Based on analysis of misclassification patterns in decoding analysis.

claim: Before association, GC neurons show no above chance peak in the cue-similarity index throughout the entire time-course.
source: While before association GC neurons show no above chance peak in the CI throughout the entire time-course (Figure 6G)
evidence: Based on cue-similarity index analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: After learning, GC neurons showed a significant peak in cue-similarity index right after cue onset.
source: after learning GC neurons showed a significant peak in CI right after cue onset
evidence: Based on cue-similarity index analysis.

claim: After learning, GC neurons showed a stronger and sustained peak in cue-similarity index starting 1.7 s after cue onset and lasting for the duration of the delay period.
source: and a stronger and sustained peak starting 1.7 s after cue onset and lasting for the duration of the delay (500 ms between cue offset and sucrose presentation) period (Figure 6H)
evidence: Based on cue-similarity index analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The sensory modality of non-gustatory stimuli is encoded throughout the stimulation period in both untrained and trained rats.
source: These results show that the sensory modality of non-gustatory stimuli is encoded throughout the stimulation period as well as following the offset of the stimulus in both untrained and trained rats.
evidence: Based on decoding analysis results.

claim: GC neurons in trained animals can encode the associability of the cue during the delay period.
source: GC neurons in trained animals can also encode the associability of the cue during the delay period.
evidence: Based on cue-similarity index analysis and decoding results.

claim: The experience of eating is inherently multimodal, involving the integration of gustatory, somatosensory and olfactory signals in a single percept called 'flavor'.
source: The experience of eating is inherently multimodal, involving the integration of gustatory, somatosensory and olfactory signals in a single percept called 'flavor' (Katz et al., 2001; De Araujo and Rolls, 2004; Spence, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: The approach to food is guided by multisensory cues that predict its availability.
source: In addition, the approach to food is guided by multisensory cues that predict its availability (Gardner and Fontanini, 2014; Kusumoto-Yoshida et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: Learning the taste-predictive value of an auditory cue increases the prevalence of auditory responses in GC.
source: Recently it was shown that learning the taste-predictive value of an auditory cue increases the prevalence of auditory responses in GC (Samuelsen et al., 2012; Gardner and Fontanini, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: GC can encode stimuli of all sensory modalities, even stimuli that have relatively little ethological relationship to taste.
source: Our experiments show that GC can encode stimuli of all sensory modalities, even stimuli that have relatively little ethological relationship to taste, like sounds or flashes of light.
evidence: Based on experimental recordings showing responses to auditory, visual, olfactory, and somatosensory stimuli.

claim: In untrained animals, each sensory modality engages a selective group of unimodal neurons in GC.
source: In untrained animals, each sensory modality engages a selective group of unimodal neurons, endowing GC with the ability to discriminate different stimuli.
evidence: Based on analysis showing majority of neurons respond to single modalities and decoding analysis.

claim: The presence of cross-modal responses in untrained animals may reflect GC's intrinsic tuning toward multisensoriality.
source: The presence of cross-modal responses in untrained animals may reflect GC's intrinsic tuning toward multisensoriality and its ability to encode different dimensions linked to food expectation.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings.

claim: Cross-modal responses in untrained animals can represent a substrate upon which learning can operate.
source: These responses can also represent a substrate upon which learning can operate (Vogels et al., 2011).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Pairing stimuli with sucrose leads to an expansion of cross-modal representations and the development of cue responses.
source: Indeed, pairing stimuli with sucrose leads to an expansion of cross-modal representations and the development of cue responses.
evidence: Based on comparison of neural responses between untrained and trained rats.

claim: After learning, fewer neurons are unimodal and more become multimodal in GC.
source: After learning, fewer neurons are unimodal and more become multimodal, suggesting that GC is now also encoding for a common property of the cross-modal stimuli, e.g., their taste-anticipatory value.
evidence: Based on analysis of convergence of responses in trained rats.

claim: After associative learning, GC can encode both the identity of different cross-modal stimuli and their associability.
source: In addition to encoding expectation, decoding analysis indicates that, after associative learning, GC can encode both the identity of different cross-modal stimuli, and their associability.
evidence: Based on decoding analysis and cue-similarity index results.

claim: The bias for odors and somatosensory stimuli in GC persists after matching the number of sessions at final performance level.
source: As Figure 3—figure supplement 2 shows, the bias toward olfactory and somatosensory stimuli persisted within this matched sample of sessions.
evidence: Based on additional analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No increase in the number of cross-modal responsive neurons was observed with increasing the number of sessions at final performance level.
source: No increase and no difference in the number of cross-modal responsive neurons were observed with increasing the number of sessions at final performance level.
evidence: Based on analysis of neuron counts across sessions.

claim: The imbalance in responsiveness to different cues might reflect the strong ecological relationship between odors, somatosensory stimuli and taste in rodents.
source: In summary, these results suggest that the imbalance in responsiveness to the different cues might reflect, at least in part, the strong ecological relationship between odors, somatosensory stimuli and taste in rodents.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings based on ecological considerations.

claim: Cross-modal responses in primary sensory cortices are not limited to border zones.
source: Recent work from alert animals, however, has shown that cross-modal responses are not limited to border zones (Lakatos et al., 2007; Iurilli et al., 2012; Maier et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: Associative learning is fundamental for shaping cross-modal responses in frontal cortices.
source: Associative learning is fundamental for shaping cross-modal responses in frontal cortices (Watanabe, 1992; Lipton et al., 1999; Fuster et al., 2000), and in subcortical areas (Yu et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: Associative learning is known to modify sensory representations in primary sensory cortices.
source: Associative learning is also known to modify sensory representations in primary sensory cortices (Zhou and Fuster, 2000; Brosch et al., 2005; Shuler and Bear, 2006; Weinberger, 2007; Grossman et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: Learning is capable of expanding the representations for all cross-modal stimuli, regardless of how much they activate GC at baseline.
source: Nevertheless, learning is capable of expanding the representations for all the stimuli, regardless of how much they activate GC at baseline.
evidence: Based on comparison of neural responses between untrained and trained rats for all stimulus types.

claim: Associative learning enhances the similarity of responses to stimuli with similar associability.
source: In addition to expanding cross-modal representations, associative learning enhances the similarity of responses to stimuli with similar associability.
evidence: Based on cue-similarity index analysis.

claim: GC's cross-modal representations are plastic and likely to be affected by conditioning with aversive gustatory outcomes or by extinction.
source: The results from trained rats strongly indicate that GC's cross-modal representations are plastic and, hence, likely to be affected also by conditioning with aversive gustatory outcomes (quinine) or by extinction.
evidence: Speculative inference based on observed plasticity in the current study.

claim: Ten female Long-Evans rats were used in the experiments.
source: The experiments in this study were performed on ten female Long-Evans rats (250–350 g; Charles River).
evidence: Description of experimental subjects.

claim: Female rats were chosen for their amenability to experiments in restraint and for consistency with previously published work.
source: We chose female rats for their amenability to experiments in restraint and for consistency with previously published work (Samuelsen et al., 2012; Jezzini et al., 2013; Samuelsen et al., 2013; Gardner and Fontanini, 2014; Liu and Fontanini, 2015).
evidence: Explanation of experimental design choice with citations.

claim: Electrodes consisted of drivable bundles of 16 individual formvar-coated nichrome micro-wires.
source: Electrodes consisted of drivable bundles of 16 individual formvar-coated nichrome micro-wires (Samuelsen et al., 2012, 2013), which were bilaterally inserted above GC (dorso-ventral: −4 mm from dura).
evidence: Description of experimental methods with citation.

claim: Movable electrode bundles were lowered approximately 200 µm after each experimental session.
source: Movable bundles were lowered ~200 µm after each experimental session allowing us to record multiple ensembles in the same animal.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.

claim: The concentrations of sucrose, citric acid and NaCl used were 0.1 M.
source: The concentrations of the four basic tastants used were 0.1 M for sucrose, citric acid and NaCl
evidence: Description of experimental methods.

claim: The concentration of quinine-HCl used was 0.001 M.
source: while a concentration of 0.001 M was used for quinine-HCl
evidence: Description of experimental methods.

claim: The auditory cue consisted of a 75 dB, 2 kHz single tone.
source: The auditory cue consisted of a 75 dB, 2 kHz single tone.
evidence: Description of experimental stimulus.

claim: The visual cue was delivered by two green LEDs with a peak emission wavelength of 575 nm.
source: Two green LEDs with a peak emission wavelength of 575 nm delivered the visual cue.
evidence: Description of experimental stimulus.

claim: The olfactory cue was 0.1% Isoamyl acetate.
source: The olfactory cue (0.1% Isoamyl acetate) was delivered via a custom-built, computer-controlled olfactometer (Verhagen et al., 2007)
evidence: Description of experimental stimulus with citation.

claim: The duration of all cross-modal sensory stimuli was 2 s.
source: The duration of all cross-modal sensory stimuli was 2 s.
evidence: Description of experimental methods.

claim: Signals were amplified, band pass filtered (300–8000 Hz), digitized and recorded at a sampling rate of 40 KHz.
source: Signals were amplified, band pass filtered (300–8000 Hz), digitized and recorded (Plexon [Dallas]; sampling rate: 40 KHz).
evidence: Description of electrophysiological recording methods.

claim: The average number of units recorded per rat was 27 ± 5.2 for the Untrained group.
source: The average number of units recorded per rat was 27 ± 5.2 and 23.6 ± 2.5 for the Untrained and Trained groups, respectively.
evidence: Description of experimental data collection.

claim: The average number of units recorded per rat was 23.6 ± 2.5 for the Trained group.
source: The average number of units recorded per rat was 27 ± 5.2 and 23.6 ± 2.5 for the Untrained and Trained groups, respectively.
evidence: Description of experimental data collection.

claim: A neuron was considered taste selective if it was responsive to at least one of the four tastes and its response varied significantly across different tastants in either magnitude or time course.
source: A neuron was considered taste selective if it was responsive to at least one of the four tastes and its response varied significantly across different tastants in either magnitude or time course.
evidence: Description of analysis method.
